https://www.dw.com/en/russian-classroom-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NE46 Patriotism has become a core part of the national curriculum since 2022 Image: Konstanin Kokoshkin/Pivcario/picture alliance Advertisement Earlier this year, several schools in Novosibirsk, a city of 1.6 million in southern Siberia, received a textbook on patriotism from the authorities. According to students, with whom DW spoke to on condition of anonymity, in the book the authors urge children to prepare themselves to die for their country. Furthermore, they equate homosexuality with pedophilia and Disney cartoons with pornography, and give instructions on how women should use their "charms." Europeans are described as "thieves, murderers and liars." The textbook, which provides "materials for spiritual, moral, and patriotic upbringing" is supposed to be used as part of "patriotism lessons" that have been on the curriculum since 2022 . Though it is not included on the national list of core curriculum books, the content reflects the Kremlin's intentions to spread propaganda in educational institutions. 'Love always involves sacrifice' One of the main topics of the book is the war in Ukraine and the idea that dying for one's country is a blessing is repeated several times: "Love always involves sacrifice," writes one of the authors. "The sacrifice of a defender of the homeland is their life." Elsewhere in the book, the authors make constant claims that Russia is better than Western countries. They also say that children are "mentally crippled" because of "computer games, Hollywood action films, pornography and Disney cartoons." They argue that European nations that used to be colonial empires legitimized "murder, lies and plunder" through the conquest and subjugation of new territories. Russia, on the other hand, "never exploited its numerous peoples," they say, but merely improved their living conditions. The book makes no mention of the culture of Indigenous peoples in what is Russia today, or of any religions other than Christianity and "Slavic paganism." This textbook is used in certain Russian schools to teach children about patriotism and other subjects Image: M. Remaevich 'More cannon fodder' For Ilya, a 16-year-old student in Novosibirsk who has read the book and whose name has been changed, the idea of dying for his country is anathema. "It's proof that the country wants more cannon fodder," he told DW, adding that "dying for the country" actually meant dying for "the president's interests and ambitions." He said that a few years ago, he had started watching the videos of Alexei Navalny, the Kremlin critic and opposition leader who died in jail in 2024 "more for fun than for any other reason." He said it was Navalny's 2021 investigation into Russian President Vladimir Putin's Black Sea palace that had first drawn his attention. But it was when the authorities decided to block access to the US platforms YouTube and Discord that he began to oppose the government. He set up a VPN out of "contrariness" he said, looking for information about other opposition figures and reading the independent media. As he found out more about the cruelty and senselessness of the war, he criticized the government more strongly. He confirmed that propaganda had become an integral part of the curriculum in the past four years. On top of the "Conversations about Important Things" that take place every Monday morning, there are now also subjects such as "Fundamentals of Homeland Security and Defense." He said that people who have taken part in the war in Ukraine are invited to lessons focusing on students' future and decisions regarding what career path to take. Even outside of the classroom, students are encouraged to be "patriotic." Ilya said that a student had been reprimanded by the principal for wearing a sweater with a slogan written in English on it. "Young man, do you realize that your sweater has words on it in the language of unfriendly countries?" she reportedly asked him. "A call to the Federal Security Service will take care of that!" Ilya also recalled that a school assembly held to mark May 9, which commemorates the Soviet Union's victory over Nazi Germany in 1945, the principal and her deputy had compared what is known in Russia as the " Great Patriotic War " to the current war in Ukraine. They had said that Russia would once again be steadfast and emerge victorious. Students are taught about being a soldier and told it is an honor to die for the country Image: Konstantin Kokoshkin/Picvario/Russian Look/Global Look Press/picture alliance 'I love freedom' Alexei (name changed), another 16-year-old student in Novosibirsk, told DW that many of his classmates avoided going to "patriotic events." He too said that the blocking of YouTube had made a difference to him. "I looked into why it was blocked," he said. "Because nothing happens by chance. And that's how my interest in politics began." That's when he realized that the authorities wanted to get rid of inconvenient citizens and suppress free speech. "I love freedom, so it was hard," he said. Ilya thinks that most students don't take the propaganda seriously. "On the one hand, we laugh about it in class, at least my friends do," he said. "On the other, we don't care. Some simply don't listen. We're very good at being quiet and not talking much about it," Dima Zicer is an educator and the author of the Russian-language podcast "Love, Don't Discipline" who moved to Estonia after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine . He told DW that "many students are happy to be part of a pro-Putin majority that doesn't think about things, according to the principle: 'We'll crush them all; we're stronger than everyone else. Everyone will be scared of us.'" He said that there was no statistical data to back his argument, but he said that he had drawn his conclusions from his extensive experience working with Russian children, as well as his communication with parents. He said that these often only became aware of how serious the situation was when their children started saying things such as "We'll crush them" or "Putin is great," as well as talking about supposed Nazis and fascists in Ukraine. Alexei and Ilya, who think differently and want the war in Ukraine to end, are worried about the unstable situation in Russia. They want to leave the country after graduating. https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/in.text: Russia’s Attacks on Europe Are Getting More Brazen and More Dangerous September 17, 2026 by Bloomberg News Over the course of the summer, Russian attacks have been pushing ever deeper into European territory. On Aug. 11, military divers destroyed two drones floating off the coast of Romania near a €4 billion ($4.7 billion) energy project. Nine days later, Bucharest scrambled two F-16s to take out a maritime drone near the same Black Sea gas platform with hundreds of workers on board. Earlier that month, German police detected an armed UAV at Leipzig airpor t, while this week NATO jets downed another unmanned aircraft that entered Lithuanian airspace from neighboring Belarus, an ally of Moscow. In all these cases, the authorities pointed the finger squarely at the Kremlin. As Vladimir Putin’s war on Ukraine grinds on with little movement on the battlefield and thousands of casualties each week, so-called hybrid attacks on Europe are increasing not just in number, but in their recklessness. Companies on the frontline find themselves caught in a gray zone between war and peace and European officials, who asked not to be named discussing sensitive issues, fear that it’s only a matter of time until there are civilian casualties. “It’s clear that the European defense industry is working in a different security environment than a few years ago,” said Kuldar Väärsi, CEO of Estonian defense firm Milrem Robotics, which was targeted by a suspected arson attack in August. “As a company whose systems are used by several NATO member states and other ally and partner nations, including Ukraine, we need to take the resultant risks into account.” Read more: Europe Struggles to Counter Russian Attacks Falling Short of War Just this week, the US Justice Department accused the Russian intelligence service of “conspiring to finance terrorism and commit murder for hire” in Europe at the behest of the Kremlin. Defense plants, public utilities, transport systems and communications networks have all been attacked, presenting Europe’s leaders with their greatest security threat in decades. So far, it’s unclear if they’re up to the challenge. “We struggle to counter so-called hybrid attacks with open societies that make it easy for the attacker,” said James Everard, former NATO Deputy Supreme Allied Commander Europe. “This is war without battle, and behind their nuclear shield Russia believes it can act with impunity, acting directly or through proxies.” The breadth and frequency of these incidents would have been unthinkable a few years ago in a continent that long considered itself shielded by NATO’s mutual-defense pact. But with President Donald Trump casting doubt on US commitment to the military alliance and Russia intensifying its war on Ukraine as winter approaches, confidence in Europe’s security now looks far less assured. Germany is the “daily target of hybrid warfare” by Russia, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Sept. 1. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said those accusations were “completely unfounded.” The past two months have seen a shift in Russia’s focus toward defense-industrial and logistics targets directly connected to support for Ukraine, according to one NATO country official, who added that this more aggressive campaign presents higher risks. With Moscow continuing to structure operations so that it can deny direct responsibility, the campaign is more significant strategically than for the physical damage caused so far, the official said. That assessment could change as Russia ups the ante with incidents such as last weekend’s drone assault at a train station near the Ukraine-Polish border as European and US dignitaries were passing through. Such attacks had been largely taboo until now, offering further evidence of a growing brazenness and willingness to risk foreign victims. Where once Russia stood accused of election interference and weaponizing migration, it’s now suspected of sabotage, arson, tampering with critical infrastructure, cyberattacks and airspace violations, including an incident last week that resulted in two civilian deaths at a border post between Ukraine and fellow EU aspirant Moldova. The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, says Europe is experiencing “a wave of increasingly kinetic hybrid attacks.” The difficulty in responding to hybrid attacks has at times led to a reluctance to blame Russia openly, both to avert escalation and avoid revealing intelligence methods, officials say. Many incidents, especially cyberattacks and hacks targeting critical infrastructure, are barely reported if at all, meaning the scale of the problem is far wider than is made public. Many arms makers in Germany are targeted by regular cyberattacks, according to a person familiar with the matter. In 2024, arsonists set fire to the home of Armin Papperger, the chief executive officer of defense giant Rheinmetall AG, and western intelligence agencies warned that Russia was plotting to kill him. He now travels with a heavy security detail and Rheinmetall has increased its overall security measures. German radar and sensor maker Hensoldt AG is increasing drone and perimeter surveillance at its plants and wants to build the infrastructure required to down drones itself, CEO Oliver Dorre said in an interview. It needs approval from the federal police to do this, and Dorre said guidelines are needed sooner rather than later, before the situation becomes worse. Poland, as a key conduit for aid to Ukraine, has suffered a spate of suspicious incidents, with multiple cyberattacks on public utilities like water, energy infrastructure and hospitals, and damage to the rail line between Warsaw and the Ukrainian border attributed to Russian intelligence. Prime Minister Donald Tusk described a fire at a plant for one of Europe’s largest drone makers, WB Electronics, in August as an “act of sabotage,” though no public link was made to Russia. Poland announced this month it’s expanding protection of its airspace and strengthening rapid-response defenses, citing the threat from “Russian provocations.” Europe’s largest weapons makers are mostly undeterred by the increasing level of Russian activity aimed at their facilities and personnel, according to a person at one such company. Security has been tightened, and lingering “muscle memory” from the Cold War is feeding a vigilance that borders on paranoia, the person said. Other key businesses are less well able to defend themselves. Achieving 100% protection of electricity networks is impossible, “especially when you may not even know what you are facing,” said Juha Räsänen, CEO of Savon Voima, an energy company in eastern Finland. “Physical security, physical monitoring, cameras and different types of detection methods are being increased all the time,” he said. “But the most important thing is that people learn to tolerate power outages.” That kind of resilience points to another reality: Russia’s campaign has so far failed to substantially reduce European support for Ukraine. The rise in high-profile incidents has instead reinforced arguments for more European defense spending, tighter counterintelligence coordination and new sanctions. As one official put it, the Kremlin’s campaign may be disruptive but is proving counterproductive for Moscow. Germany, for example, made it known after Leipzig that a delivery of additional Iris-T air-defense missiles to Ukraine is planned for September, and that Berlin will also soon provide Kyiv with several thousand strike drones. As hybrid actions move deeper into Europe, the lid is occasionally peeled back to reveal what authorities are confronting. In early September, a British man was arrested and charged under the National Security Act with giving details about drone manufacturing sites in England to a Russian intelligence unit and preparing to commit sabotage. His lawyers said his allegiance lies with the UK. That comes on the back of suspected arson attacks on former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s home, Russian submarine activity around critical infrastructure in the British Isles, and drones launched from shadow fleet vessels in UK and Irish waters, including during Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s visit to Ireland this year. Governments from London to Warsaw are scrambling to ratchet up their individual and collective responses before more serious damage spirals into open conflict with Russia. NATO is strengthening deterrence in the nations affected, officials say, but a coordinated strategy continues to elude member states. The understanding among security officials is that Putin is testing how far he can push NATO members to expose indecision among the allies while staying below the threshold that would trigger retaliation under the Article 5 collective-defense clause. Yet that probing raises the chances of miscalculation and accidents. “Russia is consistent in identifying weaknesses in NATO’s infrastructure and is willing to attempt multiple tactics and targets in a flexible and increasingly risk-taking manner,” said Emily Ferris, associate fellow at the London-based Royal United Services Institute. Ferris published a report in March on sabotage attacks attributed to Russia in NATO countries and found the alliance “unprepared.” Six months later, her verdict hasn’t changed. “In the absence of clear red lines from NATO about the consequences of attacks like this, Russia is expanding to fill the space of the uncertainty,” she said. The only time that Article 5 was invoked was by the US after the Sept. 11 attacks of 2001. Western intelligence agencies are now applying counter-terrorism methodology developed since then and the fight against al-Qaeda and Islamic State to Russian hybrid warfare, according to two officials. Russia and terror groups both use proxies, often recruited online. Hence for western agencies, there are similarities in identifying threat actors. The difference is that those recruited to Moscow’s service are not ideological, but paid. Western security officials say that Moscow is acting out of desperation after Ukraine’s drone attacks targeting energy infrastructure and logistics warehouses damaged the Russian economy. The view from Moscow is that the more painfully Ukraine hits Russia, the stronger will be the voices who want to make Europe pay. A person close to the Kremlin put it more bluntly, saying that Russia will make life hell for Europe through asymmetrical hybrid operations over its support for Kyiv. To those on the front line like the Baltic states, Russia has long since crossed any notional boundaries. “This is not hybrid, this is about explosives that can cause damage. There can be casualties. People may die,” said Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys. “If we won’t stop this, it will escalate.” Photograph: Police cars near the railway damaged in an explosion in Mika, Poland on Nov. 17, 2025; photo credit: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP/Getty Images Related: NATO Allies Foil Russian Subsea Cable Sabotage Plot War Overtakes Civil Unrest as Top Political Violence Exposure for Global Businesses Was this article valuable? Composite: Reuters Strait of Hormuz People scour strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacks container ships At least 15 vessels struck in waterway in past 10 days, with rumours that they were carrying valuable goods Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Mon 19 Oct 2026 10.48 EDT Last modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google People have been scouring the strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacked at least 15 container ships passing through the crucial waterway in the past 10 days. Some ships have been hit by drones, others by mines. On Sunday, a ship was struck by a rocket-propelled grenade launched from a small boat 75 miles (120km) north-east of the Saudi port of Jubail. The rise in Iranian attacks appears to have helped resolidify Tehran’s disputed control over the strait, as well as pushing the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil close to $108 a barrel on Monday morning. View image in fullscreen A container from the Singapore-flagged GFS Pride floats alongside small motorboats after the ship sank off the coast of Oman on 14 October. Photograph: Social media/Reuters Last Wednesday a ship travelling from Karachi, Pakistan, to Fujairah, in the United Arab Emirates , sunk after hitting a mine, according to Iranian state TV. All 21 crew members were evacuated and no injuries were reported. Dozens of its 2,500 containers were seen floating in the water. Rumours that iPhones and other expensive goods were among its cargo – fuelled by fake AI-generated photos published on social media – prompted fishers and others to investigate. One fisher told an Iranian reporter: “The Arab boatmen, who were closer to the ship, arrived earlier than the Iranians. They used stonecutters to cut the container and took whatever was there.” Col Javad Mokhtar Rezaei, the deputy head of cultural and social affairs for Iran’s cyber police (Fata), told the Tasnim news agency: “In some cases, the phones offered may actually exist, but exposing electronic components to salt water and extreme humidity can cause corrosion of internal components, damage to the boards, battery and display, and cause hidden malfunctions in the device’s performance.” Meysam Doost-Mohammadi, a spokesperson for the Iranian mobile phone Aassociation, said it would be unusual for valuable devices to be transported by ship. The bulk of the recent attacks have occurred close to the coast with Oman , a route that Iran regards as unauthorised. In the seven days to Friday 16 October, 12 vessels were attacked, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO). The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps ( IRGC) says it has the right to attack any ship that seeks to traverse the strait without its permission or with its transponders off. Officials have also ordered local fishers not to pillage the sea for luxury items, saying the goods are the property of the state. Two oil tankers were hit on Saturday, including a supertanker carrying 2m barrels of oil, according to the IRGC. The Fars news agency published a video that appears to show the tanker burning, but which cannot be independently verified. A third tanker was hit late on Sunday. It is disputed how many ships have been hit by mines or IRGC shelling. UKMTO’s weekly overview recorded 254 transits of the strait (125 outbound, 129 inbound) in the week to 14 October, approximately 70% below pre-conflict levels. View image in fullscreen A satellite image shows containers and items floating in the water after the Singapore-flagged GFS Pride sank off the coast of Oman on 14 October. Photograph: European Union/Copernicus Sentinel-2/Reuters Dr Devaraj Asir Ramesh, of Anna University in Chennai, India, warned that the region’s marine habitats faced threats from toxic debris and oil spills, while noise might have disturbed marine life. Iranian strikes on the Emirates, he said, were likely to have contaminated seagrass beds with hydrocarbons and caused auditory damage to cetaceans – marine mammals such as dolphins and porpoises – which are sensitive to loud noise that travels through the sea. Oil released by attacks on tankers at Fujairah could have caused ecological harm, he added. “Oil spills, chemical leaks and acoustic disturbances have impaired biodiversity, fisheries, aquaculture, desalination, and eco-tourism,” he wrote in the International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Sciences. View image in fullscreen Vessels in the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman. Iran has offered to open the strait in six days in return for sanctions relief. Photograph: Reuters On Friday, the Iranian president said the conflicts in Gaza and the wider Middle East had inflicted a significant toll on nature that extended beyond borders and required “international solutions”. “What has occurred in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ecocide, or environmental genocide, and it must be condemned,” Masoud Pezeshkian said. He argued that countries subjected to economic sanctions or military aggression should not be forced to shoulder the financial burden of environmental damage resulting from conflicts they did not initiate. Successive studies, mainly by US universities using satellite imagery, have warned of the dangers facing the strait. Meanwhile, the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, visited Tehran offering to act as an intermediary between Iran and Donald Trump, especially over the issue of Iran’s nuclear stockpile, which the US president insists must be addressed before he lifts his threat to attack Iran again. Iran has offered to open the strait in six days in return for sanctions relief. Russia has offered to take Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium, but Iran is reluctant to make a commitment on its nuclear programme and has not given the International Atomic Energy Agency access to its bombed nuclear sites since June 2025. Lavrov also proposed a trilateral summit between China, Russia and Iran to agree new security architecture for the strait. He said the region was on the verge of a full-scale crisis. Tehran is braced for another attack soon, especially after the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, launched a new national security doctrine on Sunday that included an emphasis on prevention and offence, including pre-emptive strikes on potential threats.
